newsitem.title: FRANCE: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND RETIRES AFTER WINNING WORLD CUP.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND RETIRES AFTER WINNING WORLD CUP.

text.p: Alpine skier Luc Alphand, who ended his most glorious season with the overall World Cup title last March, said on Thursday he was retiring to spend more time with his family.
"It was not an easy decision to take," said the 31-year-old Frenchman. "Eighty percent of the people around me wanted me to carry on but I have a family to look after."
Alphand, who has won 12 World Cup races but never a major championship, had considered carrying on until next year's Winter Olympics in Nagano, Japan.
But he said he was not certain to win and feared he might get injured again.
"You never know what can happen in one-day races and I don't want to spoil everything with another injury," said Alphand, who was once more famous for his spectacular crashes than for his successes.

"What happened to my friend Adrien probably helped me make up my mind," he said, referring to the bad accident suffered by compatriot and room mate Adrien Duvillard last January in Wengen, Switzerland.
Alphand, whose 13-year career has been hampered by a string of injuries, had established himself as the world's best speed racer over the last few seasons.
In March he became the first ever speed specialist to win the overall World Cup and the first Frenchman to do so since Jean-Claude Killy in 1968.
A junior world champion in 1983, Alphand became a member of a fast-rising gang of French skiers known as the Top Guns, along with Denis Rey, Franck Piccard and Jean-Luc Cretier.
Towards the end of the 1980s he decided to concentrate on speed racing but he spent more time in hospital rooms than on the slopes.
"I went full speed ahead and knew all the hospitals near all the courses," he said last March after his World Cup triumph. "I was so wild."

Injuries took their toll. In 1987, he injured both hips and his thigh. In 1988, he hurt his ankle. His back, wrist and shoulder were damaged in 1989. The next year, he hurt a wrist and an ankle. In 1992 he tore a pelvic muscle. A year later he tore ligaments in his knee.
His big breakthrough came in January 1995 in Kitzbuehel where he won two downhills staged on the same day at the classic Austrian course. He went on to win three successive downhill World Cup titles.
His most successful season was last winter with six victories, the downhill title and the super-G crown as well as overall victory.

"I like the idea of stopping while I'm at the top," said Alphand, who has a three-year-old daughter, Estelle, and a one-year-old son, Niels. His wife Anna Karin, who is Swedish, is expecting a third child.

"They haven't seen much of me in the last few years," said Alphand, who will work in public relations for his ski manufacturers and his home town, the French Alpine resort of Serre-Chevalier. "It's about time I spent more time with the people I love most."
